Let \(N=A+I\). Since \(R\) has characteristic \(2\),

\[
A^2=I \iff (I+N)^2=I \iff N^2=0.
\]

Also \(I+N\) is automatically invertible when \(N^2=0\), with inverse \(I+N\). So we count \(3\times 3\) matrices \(N\) over \(R\) with \(N^2=0\).

Write

\[
N=N_0+tN_1+t^2N_2,\qquad N_i\in M_3(\mathbb F_2).
\]

Then

\[
N^2=N_0^2+t(N_0N_1+N_1N_0)+t^2(N_0N_2+N_2N_0+N_1^2).
\]

Over \(\mathbb F_2\), a square-zero \(3\times3\) matrix has rank \(0\) or \(1\). There is \(1\) rank \(0\) matrix. Rank \(1\) square-zero matrices are counted by choosing image line \(L\) and kernel plane \(K\supset L\):

\[
7\cdot 3=21.
\]

Case 1: \(N_0=0\). Then \(N^2=0\) requires \(N_1^2=0\), and \(N_2\) is arbitrary. There are \(22\) choices for \(N_1\) and \(2^9\) choices for \(N_2\), giving

\[
22\cdot 2^9=11264.
\]

Case 2: \(N_0\) has rank \(1\). All such \(N_0\) are conjugate, so take

\[
J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Let \(d(X)=JX+XJ\). The condition on \(N_1\) is \(d(N_1)=0\). Solving gives

\[
N_1=\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&c\\
0&a&0\\
0&h&i
\end{pmatrix},
\]

so \(\dim\ker d=5\). Now \(N_2\) must solve

\[
d(N_2)=N_1^2.
\]

A direct multiplication gives

\[
N_1^2=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&ch&c(a+i)\\
0&a&0\\
0&h(a+i)&i
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The image of \(d\) consists exactly of matrices

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
p&q&r\\
0&p&0\\
0&s&0
\end{pmatrix},
\]

so we need \(i=0\). Thus \(N_1\) has \(2^4=16\) valid choices, and for each one \(N_2\) has \(|\ker d|=2^5\) choices. For each rank \(1\) matrix \(N_0\), this gives

\[
16\cdot 2^5=512
\]

lifts. Since there are \(21\) such \(N_0\), this contributes

\[
21\cdot 512=10752.
\]

Therefore the total number is

\[
11264+10752=22016.
\]

\[
\boxed{22016}
\]
